title: Those about to die
author: Suetonius

edition.name: Suetonius, De Vita Caesarum, vol. II (Claudius to Titus), Latin text of the Loeb Classical Library edition (J. C. Rolfe, vol. II, 1914), as presented on LacusCurtius (Bill Thayer), whose Latin pages say MCMXIII; public domain

source_text: Quin et emissurus Fucinum lacum naumachiam ante commisit. Sed cum proclamantibus naumachiariis: "Have imperator, morituri te salutant!" respondisset: "Aut non," neque post hanc vocem quasi venia data quisquam dimicare vellet, diu cunctatus an omnes igni ferroque absumeret, tandem e sede sua prosiluit ac per ambitum lacus non sine foeda vacillatione discurrens partim minando partim adhortando ad pugnam compulit.
excerpt_note: The second and third sentences of section 21.6. The edition's apparatus records a variant for "Aut non": "avete vos" ("hail to you").

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: Fūcinum: long ū, the usual dictionary quantity; not machine-checked.
pūgnam: spelled as the app lexicon spells it (DCC marks the "hidden" long vowel before gn); many textbooks print pugnam.
cunctātus: written with a short u; some dictionaries mark cūnctor. Uncertain.
Havē: the edition spells it with h; the vowel quantities (ē) are those of avē.

translation: What is more, before draining the Fucine Lake he first staged a naval battle on it. But when the fighters called out, "Hail, emperor, those who are about to die salute you!", he answered, "Or not." After that remark nobody was willing to fight, as if they had been pardoned. He hesitated for a long time over whether to destroy them all with fire and sword; at last he leapt from his seat, ran around the shore of the lake with an ugly, lurching gait, and drove them into battle, partly by threats and partly by encouragement.
translation_note: moritūrī is a future participle used as a noun ("men who are going to die"); the verb salūtant is third person: "those about to die salute you". "Aut nōn" is the reading of this edition; see the essay for the variant.

essay.t: In AD 52 the emperor Claudius staged a naval battle on the Fucine Lake in central Italy before opening a tunnel to drain it.
Tacitus says he equipped triremes and quadriremes with nineteen thousand combatants, that they were criminals, and that they fought bravely; after much bloodshed the survivors were spared.
The famous greeting comes from Suetonius, and Cassius Dio gives a Greek version of it; Tacitus does not mention it at all.

Dio's version is in the first person, "We who are about to die salute thee" in the Loeb translation, and says the condemned men then sailed through each other's lines doing as little harm as possible.
The popular Latin form morituri te salutamus, "we ... salute you", matches Dio's first person rather than Suetonius's third.
It is usually treated as the regular salute of gladiators, but H. J. Leon showed that there is no evidence for that: both ancient reports describe this one event.
The men were not gladiators but naumachiarii, fighters in a staged sea battle, and in this case condemned criminals.
So the line was probably an improvised appeal for mercy from men who expected to die, not a ritual formula.

This edition prints "Aut non", "Or not", but its apparatus records a different reading, "avete vos", "hail to you", marked with the siglum ς, which in editions of Suetonius usually stands for the later manuscripts (the page itself does not explain it).
On Leon's reading of "Aut non", the fighters took it to mean "or not about to die", that is, a pardon, which is why Suetonius says they acted as if pardoned and refused to fight.
Claudius then had to force them into battle, lurching along the shore, partly by threats and partly by encouragement.

The engineering went no better: Tacitus says that when the channel was first opened it proved not to have been dug deep enough; after it was deepened, a second show was put on, with a banquet near the outlet, and this time the rushing water carried away part of the works and caused a panic.

questions.q: Who were the men who shouted the greeting?
options: Condemned criminals fighting a staged naval battle
Professional gladiators at the Colosseum games
Sailors of the imperial fleet at Misenum
Free volunteers hoping to win a prize

questions.q: What did H. J. Leon conclude about the greeting?
options: There is no evidence it was a regular gladiators' salute
It was the standard salute before every gladiatorial show
Tacitus invented it to make Claudius look ridiculous
It was carved over the entrance to the Colosseum

questions.q: Why, according to Suetonius, did the men refuse to fight?
options: They took Claudius's reply as a pardon
The lake had already drained away
Their ships were not fit to sail
Claudius had already left the show
